subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Explain.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING INSTITUTION AND CONDUCT OF PROSECUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
This bill is designed to carry into effect three recommendations of the combines investigation commissioner which are designed to strengthen the enforcement of the Combines Investigation Act and the related legislation contained in section 498 of the Criminal Code. The bill proposes no changes in the definition of offences or in the basic pattern of the legislation. It contains a number of provisions which are intended to remove certain procedural and evidentiary difficulties that have been encountered in combines proceedings, namely, difficulties arising out of the judgment of the Ontario court of appeal in the dental supplies case.
Motion agreed to and bill read the first time.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: UTILIZATION OF CANADIAN IRON ORE-REFERENCE TO REPORT IN MONTREAL "GAZETTE"
speechtext: should like to ask the Minister of Trade and Commerce if the government has noted certain news stories, particularly one which appeared on page 7 of the Montreal Gazette of this morning, foreshadowing the building of a fully integrated steel plant in the New England states to utilize iron ore from the newly-discovered deposits in Canada? Will the government consider taking all necessary steps to protect the interests of the Canadian people in the utilization of this great resource, and place before parliament proposals for the establishment of an efficient steel industry in this country for the utilization of Canada's iron ore?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. C. D. Howe (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
subtopic: UTILIZATION OF CANADIAN IRON ORE-REFERENCE TO REPORT IN MONTREAL "GAZETTE"
speechtext:
I have looked up the clipping
Inquiries of the Ministry referred to, and I notice that it deals with a statement by the vice-president of the federal reserve bank in Boston to the effect that an integrated steel mill will be built in the New England states. The report reads:
If and when such a mill is established, there's an immediate ore supply available from Belle isle, Newfoundland.
Then the report goes on to say that, later on, the mill will be able to get ore from Quebec. I can see no reason for objecting to the building of a fully integrated steel plant in the New England states. Iron ore mines in Newfoundland have been for many years supplying iron ore to Great Britain, Germany and other European countries. Those mines are also the sole suppliers of the Dominion Steel and Coal Corporation, in Cape Breton. I am sure that if another outlet for the ore can be found we shall all be happy to see the Belle isle operation enlarged.
So far as the Labrador iron ore mines are concerned, I understand that the plans call for an initial production of 10 million tons of iron ore per year. I believe the total requirements of all Canadian steel mills total about 5,500,000 tons per year. It is obvious that our steel mills can be supplied with all the ore they require, and, if a new market convenient geographically to the mines is available, it would provide a desirable outlet for that ore.
We have an integrated steel industry in Canada, which has been expanded by nearly 100 per cent within the past ten years, and is still expanding. The Canadian industry obtains part of its iron ore requirements in Canada and part in the United States. Regardless of how much iron ore this country produced, our steel industry would continue to obtain its ore from both sources, because of the desirability of having a number of different types of iron ore with which to make the steel. Therefore, I see nothing alarming in this newspaper report, nothing that threatens in any way to jeopardize Canada's interests in iron ore or in steel.

That is dollars. No dividends have been paid on the capital Stock since issue, and no interest on the bonds since 1930. Prior to 1930 only partial interest was paid on the bonds. The operating results of the railway have not been good, particularly in the years 1943 ito 1948. I have a table which perhaps I might summarize fairly quickly. For instance, in 1943 operating revenues amounted to $319,000 and operating expenses to $304,000, but because of other expenses the net corporate income of the Temiscouata Railway Company was only $208. In 1944 the net income was $315. In 1945 there was a deficit of $272. In 1946 there was a net income of $9,821, and in 1947 a net income of $1,161. In 1948 there was a deficit of $156.
The traffic handled over the railway was small. I refer to the years 1943 to 1948. The total tonnage varied from 180,943 in 1943 to 192,081 in 1948. The greatest tonnage carried was in 1946, when it amounted to 202,223 tons. The forest products which originated on the line accounted for over eighty per cent of the freight traffic I have just mentioned. The number of passengers carried varied from 37,245 in 1943 to only 11,670 in 1948. The present train service consists of a mixed passenger and freight train on Monday, Tuesday, Thursday and Saturday between Riviere du Loup and Edmundston, and freight service only between Edmundston and Connors.
It has been evident for quite some time, at least two years if not more, that the Temiscouata railway could not continue to operate under present conditions. It has been able to operate only through assistance given by the Canadian National Railways and the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and also because of the willingness of the employees of that railway to accept subnormal wages.

ac prices arrived at by negotiation with the interests holding the proprietarial rights, and they were incorporated in the Canadian government railways. Under the authority of chapter 16, 5 George V, acts of 1915, the government acquired some nine railway lines from private companies, totalling 407 miles, at an average cost per mile of $9,191. Under the authority of chapter 22, 6-7 George Y, acts of 1916, the government acquired two additional lines of railway totalling 97 miles, at an average cost of $37,048 per mile.
Then there is the position in reference to competition. Highway competition is quite keen in that area. Several highways parallel the Temiscouata railway and bus and truck services are operated in competition with it, which have contributed in no small measure to the falling off of both passenger and freight traffic.
After giving this matter careful consideration the government requested the Canadian National Railways to purchase the Temiscouata railway at a price not to exceed $500,000. The owners, represented by the bondholders' committee in London, England, held a meeting and accepted the offer made by the Canadian National on behalf of the government, and called a special general meeting of the shareholders for that purpose. Meanwhile an agreement was drafted between the government and the Temiscouata, both of which were ratified at the special general meeting. That is the agreement referred to in the resolution, dated October 14, 1949; and parliament is now being asked to sanction it.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext:
I will explain what the Temiscouata railway is. There are two arteries of the Canadian National Railways from Quebec city to the maritimes. One is the old Intercolonial, alongside the St. Lawrence river, and the other is the Transcontinental railway, which follows the Saint John river. Between them is the Temiscouata railway, which is the last link to the east between the Transcontinental railway and the Intercolonial railway. It starts at Riviere du Loup, a town of about 9,000 on the shore of the St. Lawrence, and goes direct to Edmundston. It covers a . distance of eighty-one miles to Edmundston on the Saint John river, just across from the state of Maine. Then the railway follows the Saint John river to the west; it goes from north to south, from Edmundston to Riviere du Loup and then goes west to Connors. The whole length of the railway line is approximately 113 miles.
The Temiscouata railway has received a good deal of help from the Canadian National and the Canadian Pacific in the way of freight rate reduction. The proportion of freight rate allowed by the major railway companies to the Temiscouata railway was larger, just to give some help and to permit the Temiscouata railway to keep going. It is important to realize that both great railway companies have understood the necessity of the Temiscouata railway, and have made certain sacrifices in order to help it. The Temiscouata railway celebrates its diamond jubilee this year; it is the sixtieth anniversary of its establishment. It has given valuable service to a population which is much larger than the minister has indicated. It helps the whole county of Temiscouata, the population of which is 50,000; and it also helps the county of Madawaska, the population of which is
35,000	or 40,000.
The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton suggested that the section from Riviere du Loup to Cabano should be dispensed with. In saying that he has proved that he is a great humorist. I could not take him seriously when he said that, because he knows the country, and he knows as well as anyone else that the Temiscouata railway is rendering great service to the population.

For instance, we might speak about the competition of trucks. We can put a great deal of furniture in a truck, but no one thinks of putting telegraph and telephone poles in trucks.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext: Oh, yes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext:
In my district we regard that railway essential for heavy traffic. We need the railway. There are big industries in this area. Fraser Companies Limited have big mills at Cabano and Notre Dame du Lac. A large manufacturing plant of shoe-trees is at Notre Dame du Lac. There are many mills at Cabano and in the back country at Squatteck and in all the other places. They are all dependent on the Temiscouata railway.
I must pay a special tribute to those who built the Temiscouata railway. They had the spirit of the pioneers. It was a long time ago. The financing was done with English capital. I might explain to the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar that no shares were paid; the shares were there just for the picture in the financing until subsidies were paid by the government of Sir John A. Macdonald and other governments in the old days. Those shares were transferred as a collateral guarantee until the subsidy came. The Temiscouata railway was built, as were most railways of the time, by British capital and Canadian subsidies, because the shrewd English businessmen and the far-seeing politicians of the time understood the necessity for railways. Let me tell my hon. friend that the policy of Cartier, one of the great men of the Conservative party, was a policy of railways. He said: my policy, my program, is railways-and they must know it.
Here we have a railway which has rendered good service under unfortunate circumstances, and precisely because shares were not paid in full, as they should have been, it incurred hardships. The population needs the railway. I could show my hon. friend many resolutions passed by county councils asking for immediate consideration of this matter by the government. A delegation of big businessmen and lumbermen came here from my district to urge upon the minister and the government the importance of taking immediate action in connection with this railroad.
Now the time has come. I must express the appreciation of my constituents and of those of Madawaska to the Prime Minister, the Minister of Transport and all members of the government who have understood the seriousness of the situation and have decided that the Temiscouata railway should at once be placed under the control of the Canadian National Railways.
The area east of Quebec has been forgotten for a long time; only those places near

I believe the people in the district in question are entitled to the services of the Temiscouata railway. It does seem to me, however, a tragedy that in the past thirty-three years we have had to load up the Canadian National Railways with other lines which had been established under private enterprise and ran into difficulties. My point is that in such cases the deficits should not be loaded on the Canadian National Railways. If the management of the Canadian National states that it does not wish to take the railway over, then, as has been suggested by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, the government should make provision for any deficit so that it would not stand as a further deficit on the Canadian National Railways. That system today is responsible for capital expenditures which should be removed from it. I believe this is a matter which is under consideration by the government, and I hope something substantial may be done about it in connection with another resolution which is on the order paper.
Apparently there are other railways in the same position. One hon. member this afternoon mentioned a railway in his constituency which he would like to see taken over-and he added that it was a profitable one. In any event, in circumstances such as these the losses should be segregated from those of the national railways as a whole.

speechtext:
The question raised by the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar, and mentioned earlier by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra, is a difficult one. If we do it in this case, we have to do it in all others. Under these circumstances we would find the estimate book cluttered up with items for railway services operating at a deficit, of which there are two or three or more at the present time. This is a matter concerning which advice is being sought by the government from the royal commission on transportation, and I hope it will be able to bring in some recommendation which will be of assistance. Whether or not it would be desirable to segregate losing projects from the general operations of the Canadian National Railways is a question to which I believe the commission is giving study. It is a

problem which I am pleased to have raised at this time, but one which certainly cannot be solved in the resolution before us.

The government has now embarked upon a new policy, at the very time when a royal commission is investigating the whole transportation structure in Canada. One of the things the commission was to investigate was the financial position of the Canadian National Railways. speechtext:
I think many hon. members forget that all of these railroads were subsidized at some time or other, if not by this government at least by the various provincial governments. There is not a railroad in Canada that has not received assistance from the public treasury. The Canadian National has been referred to as a tremendous organization that took over a number of bankrupt or semi-bankrupt railroads some years ago, but the fact remains that all those railroads that were taken over had rendered great service in developing this country.
They made it possible for settlers to get into remote areas and develop the resources of the country. The fact that some of them fell upon evil days does not mean that they were not of great service to the country. The railroad now being considered has operated for sixty years in a very difficult part of Canada and no doubt has rendered great service. We seem to be in a sort of socialist era and I think the best thing to do would be to amalgamate these railroads, get them all under one management. I believe that this particular railroad could be brought under Canadian National management and with the resultant reduction of overhead and management costs it might pay its way very handsomely. I am much in support of the minister's bill.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR PURCHASE BY GOVERNMENT OF CANADA
speechtext:
I am more or less in agreement with what the hon. member for Cariboo has said. No doubt a great

deal of the development in Canada has come out of the treasury of Canada through the cost of these different units which have been amalgamated and which are now known as the Canadian National Railways. To keep this matter apart, to put it on a separate basis, would make simply another entity, another downpipe into which this chamber would have to pour more and more funds.
All of us on all sides of the house must assume our responsibility for having formed these different railroad entities into the one organization. However, it is much easier to control one organization than it is to control two or three. I am of the opinion that we are caught with this. I am of the opinion that there are people along these lines who look to this organization to give them service, and I do not know if there is much we can do about it.
I suggest to the hon. member for Cariboo that there is no other organization better able to meet the problem set out in this bill than the Canadian National Railways. It has been my privilege in days gone by to criticize the management of that railroad for extravagance and other things, but let us be sensible. What else can we do? Is it not much easier for us to sit here and criticize one unit than it would be to deal with three or four units? Let us concentrate our efforts on keeping this Canadian National organization on an orderly footing. If all these units are split up it is likely to throw the whole country into a state of chaos. Let us co-ordinate all these activities, admitting all the time that we are in a mess, admitting all the time that we are in financial difficulties with regard to the ever-mounting cost of our railroads. At the same time we should keep together and see if we cannot tear down an edge here or an edge there and make it as economical an operation as possible for those who have to pay the cost, namely, the people of Canada.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SUBSIDY TO BRITISH COLUMBIA FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM QUESNEL TO PRINCE GEORGE
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of this resolution is to grant to the province of British Columbia, the owners and operators of the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, a subsidy of $15,000 per mile for the construction of an extension from Quesnel to Prince George, the extension not to exceed eighty-two and seven-tenths miles. The Pacific Great Eastern Railway Company was incorporated in 1912 under charter granted by the government of the province of British Columbia. The charter provided for the construction of a railway from Vancouver along Howe Sound to Squamish, thence to Lillooet on the Fraser river, and then following the direction of the Fraser river to Prince George. A later provision was for a line from Prince George to a point in the Peace river block with the intention of connecting with the present Northern Alberta Railways.
The reasons for the construction of the Pacific Great Eastern were: (1) to provide an independent or direct route for the Grand Trunk Pacific Railway to the city of Vancouver; (2) to open the central portion of British Columbia; and (3) to provide an outlet for the Peace river country through Vancouver. The Pacific Great Eastern Railway purchased the Howe Sound and Northern Railway, which operated a line of railway from North Vancouver along Howe sound a


distance of seven miles, and extended it to Whytecliff, making a total distance of 12-7 miles. The connecting line to Squamish was never completed.
Major construction started from Squamish, and was slow owing to difficult construction conditions. It was further prolonged by reason of the war. By 1917 approximately 180 miles north from Squamish were completed when construction virtually stopped. In 1918 the government of the province of British Columbia acquired ownership of the railway and undertook to complete construction and operate the road. By 1919 the line was extended 211 miles from Squamish, of which 180 miles were operated. Construction was continued until 1922 when the line was completed and in operation from Squamish to Quesnel, a distance of 347-8 miles. Some construction was undertaken beyond Quesnel, but this section was not operated. In 1929 operation was discontinued on the section from North Vancouver to Whytecliff. The line between Squamish and Quesnel has been continuously operated by the British Columbia government.
The government of that province has decided to extend the Pacific Great Eastern Railway by the construction of a line from the present terminus at Quesnel to connect with the Canadian National Railways at Prince George, a distance of 82-7 miles. The estimated capital cost of the extension is $8 million, or an average cost per mile of approximately $96,700. The construction of this extension will provide traffic for the railway and assist in developing the natural resources in the area consisting of large tracts of timber suitable for lumber, newsprint, pulpwood and plywood, mining possibilities, sections of agricultural and grazing lands, hydroelectric power potentialities, and sport and recreational attractions. The government of the province of British Columbia is proposing to develop hydro power in the Quesnel area, and the establishment of a pulp and paper business there. The government of the province of British Columbia has solicited dominion aid in the construction of this railway extension, and the resolution would authorize the governor in council to grant to the government of the province of British Columbia a subsidy of $15,000 per mile towards the construction of the extension, not exceeding 82-7 miles in length. The total subsidy payable would amount to $1,240,500.
There is a precedent for this practice. In 1913 the government proceeded in the same manner for the Ontario Northland Railway, and paid a subsidy of $6,400 per mile. The act, which was assented to on the 6th of June, 1913, provided for the payment of that subsidy for certain portions of the line as mentioned

therein. If hon. members of the house are interested in looking at the precedent, the act is to be found in 3 and 4 George V, chapter 53, 1913.

Mr. Chairman, as the member for the riding in which the southern terminus of this railway is situated, I feel I should say a word or two on the resolution. The Pacific Great Eastern Railway occupies a position in the province of British Columbia quite similar to that occupied by the Canadian National Railways in Canada. While the railway is now publicly owned by the province, it was not built by public ownership but rather privately. The securities were guaranteed by the province. When the company failed the province had to take over the railway and operate it.
It has not been a very profitable operation for the province. On the contrary it has been the largest single item of expense in the provincial budget. I believe that the people of British Columbia now have over $100 million invested in the line. The main reason for this railway being a losing proposition is the fact that it is isolated. The people of British Columbia often describe it as the railway which starts nowhere and ends nowhere. The hon. member for Cariboo, who represents the village of Quesnel in the northern section served by the railway, and I, representing the village of Squamish at the southerly end, might quarrel with this description, but the fact remains that the Pacific Great Eastern Railway does not connect with any other railway on this continent.
The original intent behind the railway was, however, a good one. The existing railway lines in British Columbia generally all run east and west. The most southerly line is the Kettle valley line of the C.P.R. which enters British Columbia at the Crowsnest pass just north of the United States border, and continues across British Columbia skirting that border. The main line of the C.P.R. comes into the Kicking Horse pass a little west of Banff, proceeds to Kamloops, and then down the Thompson and Fraser rivers to Vancouver. The next line, which is a part of the Canadian National system, is the old Canadian Northern line which, at Jasper, goes 45781-921
Pacific Great Eastern Railway through the Yellowhead pass, and then to Kamloops and down the same route as the C.P.R. The old Grand Trunk line, now also a part of the Canadian National system, goes through the Yellowhead pass and proceeds straight west to the ocean port of Prince Rupert. The promoters of the P.G.E. therefore believed that there was an opportunity for a north-south line, cutting across these other lines and stretching from Vancouver into the northeast corner of the province, the area commonly called the Peace river block.
The railway was actually begun in the city of North Vancouver, which is on the north shore of Vancouver harbour; and, as the minister said, it continued some thirteen miles to the community of Whytecliff. Twenty miles of mountainous country then intervened, and no attempt was made to build the railway over that area. A new start was made at the small village of Squamish, at the head of Howe sound; and, as the minister stated, some 347 miles of railway were built in a general northeasterly direction, through the Lillooet country, through the Cariboo country, to the town of Quesnel. As the minister said, the ultimate hope was to connect with the northern line of the Canadian National at Prince George, which is roughly in the centre of our province though we generally think of it as in northern British Columbia.
One of the difficulties faced by the P.G.E., of course, is the fact that because of its isolation, because neither its terminal at Squamish nor the terminal at Quesnel has any other railway serving it, it has not had the traffic which it might expect. At various times various provincial premiers have tried to sell the P.G.E., either to private railway lines or to the Canadian Pacific or to the Canadian National. These latter two lines never showed much interest in it, no doubt for the reason that it did not connect with the existing Canadian National or Canadian Pacific systems. When Byron Johnson became premier of British Columbia in 1947 he declared that if he could not sell the P.G.E. he would try to complete it, so we would not have it as a white elephant on our hands for all time. The northern gap between Quesnel and Prince George now is being completed, a distance of some 82 miles through country fortunately not as difficult as the southern end. The estimated cost of completing this gap is around $8 million. When completed it will give the P.G.E. its first link with some outside railway line, connecting as it will with the Canadian National transcontinental system to Prince Rupert at the town of Prince George. This will help the P.G.E. and also the C.N.R.,

Pacific Great Eastern Railway which will then have an exclusive opportunity to carry on its lines the traffic coming from the great Cariboo country.
Having announced this plan and construction having actually started, Premier Johnson then asked for federal assistance. I was very glad to give him what support I could. He first asked for an interest-free loan for the period of construction of the line, to commence bearing interest once the line was in operation. It was not thought desirable to set a precedent like that but, as the minister has just pointed out, it was found that in 1912 or 1913 the federal government of the day did help the government of Ontario with a subsidy of $6,400 a mile in the construction of the T. & N.O. railway. I think hon. members will agree that a subsidy of $6,400 a mile at that time would be at least equivalent to a subsidy of $15,000 a mile in these times.
As I have said, upon completion of this construction the P.G.E. will extend from the sea at Squamish to Prince George. That will be of great assistance to the Canadian National Railways, because it will mean opening up all central British Columbia as a traffic tributary to the northern line of that railway. The federal government, however, is giving still more assistance than this. It is expected that a greatly increased amount of traffic will flow south to Squamish when this new territory between Quesnel and Prince George is tapped. When the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Murray) speaks I am sure he will detail the many resources of that area, where there are a great number of small sawmills, as just one example. So larger docking facilities will be required at Squamish, particularly an assembly dock at which the output of these small mills can be collected and sorted for deep-sea shipment to export markets. The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) was very helpful in this respect. In the supplementary estimates this fall the Department of Public Works has included an initial appropriation of $100,000 for the construction of such as assembly dock, the total cost of which is estimated at half a million dollars.
The P. G. E., of course, will never be a profitable operation until the other gap is also completed, that is the gap between the village of Squamish and the city of Vancouver. This is not included in the present plans. The country between Squamish and North Vancouver is quite mountainous; construction would be extremely expensive at this time, and present traffic would scarcely warrant it. However, Premier Johnson has announced that he will build a highway between Squamish and North Vancouver, so this railway at least will have a bus and truck outlet from its terminal at Squamish to the city of North Vancouver.

I want to warn hon. members, however, that when this subsidy of $15,000 a mile for this construction is passed, I do not think it will be the last time this house will be asked to help in the extension of the P.G.E. Premier Johnson's avowed purpose in connection with that railway is to do what was originally intended; that is, push it through the Rocky mountains into the Peace river block, where there is great traffic in wheat and in the finest anthracite coal in Canada, and where there are also potential oil fields. At the present time the Peace river block of Alberta and British Columbia is served by the Northern Alberta railway; but from the town of Prince George in British Columbia to Dawson Creek at the end of the line, traffic now must travel back to Edmonton for a total of 947 miles. In other words, wheat moving to Prince Rupert has to travel this distance of 947 miles, whereas the actual distance between the two points is only 160 miles. Completion of the next link between Prince George and Dawson Creek will shorten the rail haul from the Peace river block to the Pacific coast by some 750 miles. At the present time the provincial government is building a road between Prince George and the Peace river block, but heavy freight such as wheat and coal will never be moved efficiently by truck; it will require a railroad.
Once that is done, of course, there will be need for much greater port facilities at the town of Squamish, including grain elevators and coal docks. In addition, this will provide sufficient traffic to justify the construction of the last link between Squamish and North Vancouver.
As the minister pointed out, this railway has trackage facilities within the city of North Vancouver, and eventually there is no doubt that this last twenty miles between Squamish and Vancouver will be bridged by a railway not along the sea but down Capi-lano valley following the old logging railways into North Vancouver. This will be of very great importance to our own system, the Canadian National, because it will mean a three-way link with that system: a link at Vancouver, a link up in Prince George, and then a link away up in the Peace river country, with the Northern Alberta railway. It will give the Canadian National traffic in British Columbia which that line has never had.
I want to just mention this briefly, because when we are passing this appropriation I think we should be fully aware of all the implications, since we are committing ourselves to a policy of subsidizing the extension of this provincial railway. Today British Columbia is pretty well a C.P.R. preserve as far as the most lucrative freight traffic

is concerned. The Canadian Pacific were first in the field, of course. When they came in with their main line to Port Moody, on Burrard inlet, they soon found they could do better if they moved further down, so they extended their main line 13 miles to the present site of the city of Vancouver. Nowhere along that waterfront are the C.P.R. lines more than 50 yards from the water, so they have a monopoly of the service on the Vancouver waterfront. As a matter of fact almost all the waterfront was owned by the Canadian Pacific. Since 1886 they have sold some of it to private concerns and some to the national harbours board, but the fact remains that as far as the south shore of Vancouver harbour is concerned it is pretty well a C.P.R. preserve. They got more than that. To make quite sure nobody else would have an approach to Vancouver they built a spur to the city of New Westminster, then came down the Fraser river to encircle Vancouver, so the city is completely surrounded by the railway. On the other hand the closest the Canadian National comes to Vancouver is some 15 miles, on the other side of the Fraser river at Port Mann. Our national railway actually has to come in over a United States line to reach the terminal in Vancouver; and that terminal is not on the waterfront. However, the national harbours board has a harbour board railway which does connect with the C.N.R. and go over to the north shore of the harbour.
The early leaders of the C.P.R. had thought they had completely bottled up Vancouver by having the Vancouver side of the harbour and the Fraser river as C.P.R. domain. They had forgotten that eventually a bridge would be built across the harbour to North Vancouver. The members from that area will recall how the C.P.R. blocked as determinedly as possible the construction of a railway bridge and the Lions Gate bridge. Those bridges were built and the harbour board railway does form a link over to North Vancouver. It connects with the P.G.E. North Vancouver yards.
I intend to advocate strongly that the Canadian National take over the Vancouver harbour board railway, so that the Canadian National will have the same domain on the north shore of Vancouver harbour that the C.P.R. has on the south shore. I am glad to say that this shore is now principally owned by the national harbours board. Then, when the P.G.E. links North Vancouver with Squamish, the Canadian National will not only have the north shore of Vancouver harbour as its domain, but it will have a profitable feeder line striking up through central British Columbia tapping the Lillooet and Cariboo district and linking it with the
Pacific Great Eastern Railway Canadian National at Prince George. It will link this part of British Columbia with the Peace river country by means of the main line of the Canadian National and the Northern Alberta Railways. This profitable line should then be bought from the people of
B.	C. by the C.N.R.
This investment which we are now making in the P.G.E. has long been needed. I believe it will be well worth while. Premier Johnson is to be congratulated on being the provincial premier who, at last, is doing something positive about the P.G.E. I think this federal government is to be congratulated also on helping him in this effort to expand the P.G.E.

Someone has said he failed to give it away: I do not know, that may also be true. As I have said, I believe the building and operation of this railroad is beyond the financial capacity of the province of British Columbia. I am sure that sooner or later we shall find that out. There is a large investment there now but it will be a still larger investment eventually, and some day this government will have to step in and take over that road. We might as well face that today as face it in five or ten years' time.
Why do I say it is beyond the capacity of the province of British Columbia? I admit at once the possible wealth of the area that is going to be tapped by the present extension- Quesnel to Prince George. Perhaps there is still greater wealth in the section-Prince George to the Peace river country. I believe that Canadian railways are going to be in a difficult position in the next few years. This is important for us as members of parliament, because if there is any country in the world in which railroads are essential, it is Canada. Owing to the commodities that are carried over our railways and the size of the country, railways in Canada are essential. Then we must make up our minds about one or two things. Either we are going to pay subsidies to our railways so that they can operate, or we are going to provide revenue for the purpose by higher rates. Here is where we meet the greatest difficulty: The competition facing railroads is increasing every day. The bus, freight truck and air line are faster and more mobile than the railways. The result is that they are taking the cream of the passenger, express and freight traffic. The only thing that goes over the railways is the long haul, heavy

material that cannot be carried easily by truck or aeroplane. All the good paying freight, express and passenger traffic now moves over the transportation systems I have mentioned. As roadbuilding is improved-and there has been considerable improvement in roadbuilding in British Columbia during the past three or four years and there will be more in the future-that competition will increase.
I think the time has arrived when this government and the government of British Columbia should be realistic in the matter and start discussions with the Canadian National Railways. I think some arrangements should be made with the Canadian National Railways with the view of that company taking over the Pacific Great Eastern railway. As I said, we shall have to subsidize the railroads in any case. I think probably the ultimate solution is to co-ordinate all railroads and air traffic and have one complete system. That perhaps is in the future, but may not be so far in the future as we think. Before we put much more money into subsidies I think we should know exactly what we are doing, where we are heading and what the ultimate cost is going to be.

As the member for the district through which the northern reaches of the P.G.E. are being extended I suppose it would be my duty to say something in support of this measure. The hon. member for Coast-Capilano has ably and brilliantly set out most of the facts and I would be duplicating what has already been said if I went over the early history of that railway. It was launched by the Conservative government of British Columbia and by a distinguished statesman, the late Sir Richard McBride. Although I happen to be identified with the opposing party, the longer I live the greater appreciation I have of the splendid vision and the statesmanlike character of the late Sir Richard McBride. It is true that there have been deficits and that the railway is not in a flourishing condition. Yet last year it paid $1 million in revenue, paid its operating expenses and paid for extensive improvements as well on the short section of it which is now built. But it stands as a living memorial to those who built it, and a rebuke to those who procrastinate, who are afraid to move forward, who see all the hazards and difficulties in that part of the country but have not the enthusiasm and youth of my friend the hon. member for Coast-Capilano, and the courage to step forward with a project which was well thought out in the beginning and which within the lives of men in this parliament will prove to be one of the greatest assets in the Dominion of Canada.

This railroad will be connected at Prince George with the Canadian National Railways; that action of course will vitalize it and will also vitalize that western portion of the Canadian National Railways from Jasper to the coast which is now not getting the sort of assistance it should have. That is an extremely rich part of Canada, yet the railroad service from Jasper to Prince Rupert, B.C., is of a limited character, and the required energy is not being put forward in developing the industries tributary to it.
I have heard some reference to the Canadian Pacific Railway. While I am no champion of the Canadian Pacific Railway, I want to say that when they put their line through southern British Columbia their directors and their men went in and developed the coal, the mines, the sawmills and the natural resources of that country, rightly or wrongly, and they laid the foundation for what exists in British Columbia today.
The great mining operation at Trail, the Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company of Canada, had it not been for the genius of the late James J. Warren and the men who were around Shaughnessy, would be an abandoned mineral claim today instead of being the great operation which it is, employing thousands of men and pouring wealth into British Columbia and this country, being one of the greatest metallurgical plants on the face of the earth.
Up in northern British Columbia there are resources equal to those in the Kootenay country. All we need is to have operating our railways men with the imagination and genius of those who launched the railways elsewhere in British Columbia. As to losing money on this division, I repeat what I said a few minutes ago in this chamber, namely, that there never was a railway started in Canada which was not assisted either from the dominion treasury or from the treasury of one of the provinces. I will challenge any hon. member to check up on any of them and show me one instance in which lavish grants of money or great grants of land were not made. One needs to step only a few feet from the entrance doors of this building to see the Rideau canal. How did it come into being? Why was it built?

As has been pointed out, the hon. member for Calgary West knows a good deal about oil. However his knowledge of transportation may have some gaps which should be filled in-and which I shall endeavour to do.
In the Cariboo range country there are, in extent, some of the largest cattle ranges in Canada. Those are the people in whose position I am most interested this afternoon because they have no adequate outlet by rail to their market in Vancouver. They have no adequate railway communications over which they can get feed grains. Their normal outlet for cattle to market would be through Vancouver. The place to which they would look for their feed grain required to bring their cattle to a marketable condition is the Peace river district.
Perhaps the hon. member for Calgary West, with his great knowledge of logic, will tell me which of those aspects is the more important-because, frankly, I confess that for my own part I cannot decide whether it is more important to complete the first outlet to the market, or more important to complete the line inland so as to prepare the cattle for market.
I do know however that we are now commencing with the construction of the railway to Prince George. It seems logical therefore to look as a next step for the completion of

the railway up into the Peace river area. The hon. member for Cariboo has dealt with some of the resources of that country. It has been pointed out that that particular area is served at the moment only by the Canadian National Railways main line through Prince George up to Prince Rupert.
I would leave with the committee this point for consideration:	It seems to me high
time that the Canadian National Railways took a greater interest in the Pacific Great Eastern. I do not altogether agree with what was said by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano when, as I understood him, he implied that the Canadian Pacific had a virtual monopoly of the productive freight in British Columbia. Of course members from the coast and the interior of the province of British Columbia find to our cost sometimes that some people tend to think of the province as centering around Vancouver, and they forget the great productive areas of the interior of the province which produce large quantities of paying freight.
The Canadian National now serves the Okanagan fruit country and the lumbering country of the northern North Thompson valley, and the Prince George area. It serves of course the commercial and industrial plants of New Westminster and the Fraser valley, as well as sharing with the C.P.R. the freight revenues from the Fraser valley agricultural land. So the Canadian National has a very considerable stake in British Columbia.
The result of this expansion of the Pacific Great Eastern is to link that railway up with the Canadian National at Prince George. It it, in a sense, a gift to the C.N.R. I certainly hope the national railways will no longer continue to wait for things to fall into their lap in connection with this particular railway, and that they will show that interest in it which its potentialities as a revenue-producing line fully justify.
I trust the management of the Canadian National on their part will work in cooperation with the province for the completion of the railway up into the Peace river. In turn, I hope that they will press for, and cooperate with the province in the eventual completion of the railway to Vancouver, to link up with the other terminal of the Canadian National.
I have not much more to say. This is a project which in my view has been too long delayed. I turn to the debates of 1946 when the former member for Cariboo raised the subject. One is amazed upon looking at the record to find how often the extension and completion of the Peace River Railway has been promised, and how unfortunately 45781-93
Pacific Great Eastern Railway promises have exceeded performance. It was pointed out in the debate that at one time the late Sir Henry Thornton promised to build a line into the Peace river country when the export production of wheat reached 10 million bushels. That figure has long been reached and passed, it being now away past 20 million bushels; but we are still waiting for the rail link with the Peace river.
I support this resolution on three grounds. First, because it will provide an intermediate link on the railroad which will help to develop our province. Second, because it will be a step in the development of our railroad system which will connect our interior with the prairies and Peace river markets, thus enabling our cattle ranchers to bring in their feed grain at reasonable rates from the logical place in which to get it. Third, because it will be one more step in the completion of the railroad to provide those people with an outlet to their logical market in Vancouver.

The presidents and boards of directors of those railroad companies knew perfectly well that the tremendous natural resources in that north country would have to move east over either of their railroad lines. They knew that if and when the provincial government or some private organization eventually completed that line their railroad lines would benefit. That being axiomatic, it is natural that they were prepared to wait until such time as these products did begin to move down to the ocean terminals at Vancouver or North Vancouver.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR SUBSIDY TO BRITISH COLUMBIA FOR CONSTRUCTION OF LINE FROM QUESNEL TO PRINCE GEORGE
speechtext:
I want to support the resolution as it has been proposed by the Minister of Transport. I was interested in the speeches already made on this matter and am in full agreement with practically everything that has been said. I do not represent a constituency through which the proposed line will run, but I do represent a district which will contribute, perhaps indirectly, to the success of the new line when it is built.
The full value of the Pacific Great Eastern railway can never be realized until it is finally linked up with the Northern Alberta Railways, as the hon. member for Coast-Capilano so well said. That being the case, I can assure the minister that he has not heard the last of the requests for subsidies for railroads. He is going to hear more of these in the future, not only from those people who are determined to see a link built between Prince George and Dawson Creek, but also from those who are determined to see a link built between Hines Creek on the north side of the river and perhaps Hazelton and Prince Rupert to the west.
We are up against a real problem there and I should like to draw this to the attention of hon. members who may not know the situation. Northern Alberta Railways operate between Edmonton and Dawson Creek on the south side of the Peace river. There is a branch running from McLellan, just above Lesser Slave lake, up through Peace river 
and into Hines Creek on the north side of the river. A number of years ago this line was purchased by the Canadian Pacific and the Canadian National and has since been operated under their joint ownership but still under the name of Northern Alberta Railways. Because of the fact that both great railways of Canada are interested in its ownership and management, neither of them can ever come in and threaten the monopoly that exists. There has never been any serious threat from highway competition to the monopoly that exists under the Northern Alberta Railways owned jointly by the two great transcontinental systems. That situation is gradually being improved as British Columbia and Alberta build better highways. We hope that some time the competition will be great enough to needle the two old companies into doing something about the extension of these branches and filling the gaps so that there will be a northern system linking up with Prince Rupert north of the river and back into Saskatchewan, as has been so well put before the house on various occasions by the hon. member for Athabaska.
One thing that the minister ought to take into consideration is this. The fact that there is a monopoly today will require that the government take rather unusual action to get something done about the extension of these routes. There is no doubt in my mind that the traffic is already there. As the hon. member for Kamloops has so well stated-and it is a fact-the Peace river country today is producing over 20 million bushels of wheat a year, and that is only one product. It is also producing millions of bushels of oats and barley, thousands of head of livestock, much pulpwood and lumber, and in many sections seed production is now reaching great volume.
Have the railways lost their pioneering spirit? Have they grown fat and lazy in their middle age? They must be needled into a more venturesome spirit. I wonder if it would not be well to call in question their right to hold a charter if they do not get busy and fill these gaps so that there may be a western outlet, and thus prevent the long backhaul of over 500 miles around through Edmonton and out to the Pacific coast, where much of the produce has to go. If I were in the minister's seat today I would seriously consider calling their charters in question.

Apparently he has not followed the rate discussions which have taken place before the Board of Transport Commissioners for Canada in times past as to the freight on coal to eastern Canada from areas much closer than this will be. The simple fact is that the freight on a ton of coal from that area to Toronto would be well above the $8.55 which is the rate from a closer point, even with a subvention paid by the dominion government to producers of coal in nearer areas. Therefore-and I speak most respectfully because I think the speech made by the hon. member was a fine one-with the exception of a market on the Pacific coast I do not think the coal we shall find there will be of any use to the rest of the Dominion of Canada. The prairies themselves produce the kind of coal they want, and I cannot see that within my time in any event we will be putting British Columbia coal into the heavy market here in central Canada.
Then someone spoke a moment ago about our having this railway, and the tremendous benefit it would be to the Canadian National and Canadian Pacific. Well, it has been lying at their doorstep all these years; and while the hon. member for Peace River may be able to say that they have lost their pioneering spirit-as a matter of fact they have lost their shirt with it-and are afraid to take a chance, I do not think they are so dumb that if it

Now I put forward this proposition. It seems to me that we are now embarking upon a major venture, namely the revival of the subsidization of railway construction. If that be so, a great broad question immediately presents itself, as to whether it should not be taken over by the system we already own, which has very able men at its head. In fact some of them are so able they can go to New York and make speeches concerning things about which they know nothing. But I make that point, in regard to who is to be in charge of the operation of this line.
I conclude by saying I believe that is something to which a great deal of consideration might be given. No doubt the minister will be able to tell us that he has already considered that point, and will give his reasons for adopting this method rather than the one I have suggested. Finally, Mr. Chairman, I believe that even at considerable cost we should try to do something for those pioneers who have gone into this area, some of whom are from seventy to ninety miles from railhead, who bring in their goods as best they can and ship what they produce an extra five hundred miles around through to Edmonton. That is by Canadian National of course; much of it goes around through Calgary, because hon. members will find that the freight rate from Edmonton to Vancouver direct is exactly the same as the rate through Calgary. The people who have gone in there have done splendid things. They have won the highest prizes in the world with their wheat and other grains. They need encouragement, and the opening up of the area will do immense good not only to the people immediately involved but to all Canada.
Just in order to bring the hon. member for Kamloops up to date on my knowledge, or lack of it, in connection with railways, let me tell him that in 1905, when the only issue was the construction of the Grand Trunk Pacific railway, I supported my uncle, D. W. Bole of Winnipeg, who beat Sanford Evans. I was then a good Liberal; but I had done that much politically before he was born, so at least I had that much of a start.

Pacific Great Eastern Railway there and Regina or Winnipeg? Can anyone say that the coal produced in this area can be absorbed along the line?

Before the minister replies to those questions, there are two questions I should like to place before him. Some remarks have been made this afternoon which were rather disparaging to the Pacific Great Eastern Railway. I think it would be unfortunate if the members of this house were left with the impression that the railway is nothing but a white elephant. It has had a great deal to do with the opening up of the interior of British Columbia. It is the most friendly railway in the country and I always enjoy riding on it. That has been discovered not only by the people of British Columbia; many tourists from the United States ride on the railroad because it is so different from the transcontinental lines. It has an attraction for the people from the United States as a railway on which to take a holiday trip. As the line is extended to the north, that will be even more true.
One other feature which the member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Sinclair) did not mention was the agreement between the province of British Columbia and the Grand Trunk Pacific to the effect that passengers and freight destined for Vancouver would be routed over the Pacific Great Eastern via Prince George. That was one of the main reasons why the province of British Columbia went ahead with the railway. When the Grand Trunk Pacific got into financial troubles and was eventually taken over by the Canadian National Railways, the main line to Vancouver went from Red Pass Junction down through Kamloops over the line of the old Canadian Northern. All that freight and passenger traffic which would have gone over the Pacific Great Eastern from Prince George to Vancouver was lost to the provincial government railway. The dominion certainly has a moral obligation to help the Pacific Great Eastern Railway, in addition to what benefit will be gained by the dominion as a whole through the help given to the railway. I hope that this payment of $15,000 for a few miles will not be considered as settling any obligation that the dominion may have.
Turning now to my two questions, I should like the minister to tell me what the policy

Pacific Great Eastern Railway of the government is with regard to subsidizing the road from Prince George north. Personally, I believe the government should be willing to offer the same amount of subsidy to the British Columbia government for construction from Prince George north into the Peace river country. It is almost unbelievable that a progressive people such as the Canadian people would not have insisted on a western outlet from the Peace river country many years ago. The minister's reason for taking over the Temiscouata Railway was to aid settlers. Thousands of settlers have gone into the Peace river country and been left to fend for themselves. I am asking what the policy is to be with regard to subsidizing the road north of Prince George.
The second question has to do with a proposal which is receiving consideration in the United States. It has to do with building a railway from Prince George to Alaska. I have seen a press dispatch dated October 26, under the heading "Bill for Railroad Canada to Alaska Signed by Truman". That is not a very accurate heading, but apparently what has happened is that the President has signed a bill which gives him the power to negotiate with the Canadian government with a view to extending the railway system which will now terminate at Prince George to the territory of Alaska. It further gives him power to cause surveys to be made, plans, specifications, cost estimates and budget requests to be prepared for the purpose of constructing a railroad connecting the existing railroad system terminating at Fairbanks, Alaska, with this railroad system extending from Prince George to Alaska.
A few days ago I asked the following questions of the government:
Have there been any negotiations between the government of Canada and the government of the United States concerning the construction of a railway through Canada to Alaska?
Have any surveys been made or authorized by the Canadian government in connection with such a railway?
The answer to question No. 1 was as follows:
There have been no formal negotiations, but informal discussions took place in September and October, 1942.
That was seven years ago, and apparently there have been no negotiations since that time.
The answer to the other question was:
Yes, the Canadian government authorized the United States army engineers to make a survey in 1942.
I do not know whether the United States engineers actually made that survey. I suggest that we should have from the minister some information concerning this United States proposal, because it seems to be one
[Mr. Green.l
which might be of great interest to Canada. Half of the province of British Columbia lies north of the main line to Prince Rupert. Everyone in British Columbia therefore is vitally concerned with developments in that part of the province.

Mr. Speaker, since the last debate of the house upon bills of this nature, I have inspected some of the bills and some of the evidence in cases that had been taken. Then I went to the room on the other side of the building where a case was in progress. It happened that when I went there the case was being opposed.
I sat during the morning session and heard the evidence given at that time. I was unable to go back in the afternoon, but I discovered afterwards that the committee had divided on the question of whether or not a divorce should be granted, by a vote of four to three. Since then I have been told by a member of the committee that further evidence has come to light in that particular case indicating that one of the witnesses had not been telling the truth. Although the bill was sent over here, an application is going to be made to have it sent back so that this evidence can be taken and the committee consider the case again in the light of the further evidence being advanced.
So I think we can say that the cases being put before the house tonight, when we have no information at all about them, constitute something like a farce.
Did you attend the committee meeting?
No, because I did not know it was on. I did not receive notice of it.
It is in Votes and Proceedings.

In another case which I examined I noticed that the parties had celebrated a marriage in New York. They came back to live in Montreal and had another celebration of marriage there. They had a disagreement before the second marriage, and ten days later they separated, with the result that proceedings for divorce were subsequently taken. From my examination of the evidence it seems to me that there was collusion between the parties notwithstanding the fact that it had been sworn that there was not.

No.

I think the hon. member might reserve his remarks until that particular bill is before us. Might I suggest to the hon. member that the question he is raising with regard to collusion might be raised when the bills go to the committee on miscellaneous private bills, to which they will be referred if they receive second reading tonight.

Mr. Speaker, in years past I have been more or less pronounced in my views, particularly in respect to the way we have had to deal with divorces from two of the provinces. I do not agree altogether with the member of the private bills committee when he says that it is only a matter of form to put these bills through this house. As the House of Commons we perform a particular function. These bills constitute part of the law of the land. They represent the breaking up of a marriage in order that the principals may be legally married again. Whether this procedure is formal or not, we have a perfect right to prevent these bills from becoming law. That is our privilege as members of the House of Commons.
I must raise my voice in respect to the method used to deal with divorce bills. During the course of about three minutes tonight 82 of these bills were dealt with, and there are 29 of them in the next batch that is being presented to us. Within a very few minutes a total of 110 odd bills will have gone through. As far as this procedure is concerned, this chamber could certainly be described as a divorce mill.
Private Bills-Divorce
It is true that the evidence is heard, and I think thoroughly, in the Senate committee on divorce. It is true also that members of the House of Commons have a right to go there to hear the evidence without the privilege of discussing it. When these bills are brought before the committee on miscellaneous private bills any hon. member can attend, but he cannot ask questions except with the consent of the committee which I suppose would be granted. The committee on miscellaneous private bills does not go into the evidence although it has the privilege of doing so.
The fact that the entire parliament of Canada, both lower and upper houses, has to deal with a subject like this is nauseating to me. We have implored the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) and the government to devise some other way whereby divorce bills from these two provinces could be dealt with. I think that divorce comes under the heading of property and civil rights, which are provincial matters. If I am not right, some member of the legal profession can say so. However, that is a minor point.
Some other method should be used to deal with these bills. As far as I am concerned, if the issue has to be forced it can be forced by simply voting against the bill. If we turned down a couple of hundred of them in a batch, you bet your life something would be done. That is all I have to say tonight.

Mr. Speaker, as it seems to be out of order to ask questions I should like to say a few words on this motion. Twenty minutes of the time of the house has been taken up tonight with divorce bills. I do not know why the people of Fraser Valley elected me, but they certainly did not elect me to act as a judge on divorce bills.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

judgment of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada. I believe that even in Saskatchewan there are judges who are capable of ruling in the best interests of everybody. There are important bills being brought forward by some United States interests that possibly may come up before nine o'clock.
I do not think I was elected to sit as a judge on divorce matters. If I was, I wish I had been left in Coast-Capilano or somewhere else out there. We can joke all we like about this, but the fact remains that the rights of the children may be involved and they should be of primary importance. No mover or seconder of any of these measures has told us what is to happen to the children or what alimony is to be paid.
We are told that that is of no importance because a certain committee of the other place, which must not be mentioned because of some legal rule, has considered these applications.
The rule of stare decisis.

"Subnormal" might be a good word. We are not allowed to mention it. I think any member is derelict in his duty if he has a family of his own and does not care a snap what happens to the children of his own or of somebody else's family. In my opinion it is no argument at all to bring a bill before this house and say that the matter has been judged in some other place by a certain committee. Let the sponsor of the measure come before the house and say what is the reason the divorce is being granted.

Certainly.
How could any member, unless he had a colossal memory, remember the evidence in all these cases and prepare himself to bring it before the house?

Family allowances, due to the great government we have, of which I am one of the firmest supporters and builders.
I believe in the sanctity of marriage, and I believe our divorce laws are not what they should be. I do not think one and only ground for divorce in Canada is sufficient. I think the Criminal Code ought to be amended to cover the situation. I am not a lawyer, but I believe it should be amended. I believe that no hon. member should advance some fifty bills at one time-you will have a chance over there when I am finished-and frankly admit that he knows nothing of the details, nothing of the parties concerned, and ask us to pass these bills without further information. More so-called important bills may come up before nine o'clock, but I do not think they are as important as these bills. In one case you are dealing in dollars and cents. Just a moment; I may be called to order by the Speaker but not by anyone else in this chamber. How many children are concerned in this case? I am surprised that some of the junior members of this parliament are not interested in the welfare of the children of Canada, as they should be. I am sorry I did not understand your previous ruling, Mr. Speaker. I have the greatest admiration for the province of Quebec; some of the finest cheese in the world is produced in that province.
Order. I hardly think it is in order, while dealing with one of these private bills, to discuss the whole question of divorce in Canada.
Question.

Just a moment. I do not mind being called to order by the Speaker, because after all he presides over this house, but certainly I am not going to be called to order by a junior member from Windsor or anyone else.
I am not calling anyone to order, if the hon. member is referring to me; and I am the member for Essex West.

Has the hon. member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) concluded his remarks? Shall the motion carry?

On division.

No, Mr. Speaker; not even on division. I am still speaking to the bill chosen by my hon. friend, No. 106, which has to do with the divorce of two people. I hope I shall not transgress your ruling when I say-because more people than you, sir, are listening to me this evening- that I believe people living in difficulty and trouble should have some way of separating from one another. That is just a silly thought that occurred to me, and I hope in expressing it I have not breached the ruling you just gave.

Private Bills-Divorce
The point I am so anxious to bring out is that I do not think our problem here is so much these individual cases, though in the strict interpretation of the rules I am very much inclined to agree with what you said. I do think perhaps you are being a little strict, as a result of your long association with this House of Commons and having so often seen what is going on here tonight. However, I am anxious to make my personal position plain. Someone like the hon. member for Yorkton (Mr. Stewart) may say that I am speaking to my constituents. He spoke to his constituents during his whole address the other evening and did not say a word to anyone else; but I hope I do not transgress even that rule.
It seems to me our problem is not so much the rights or wrongs of this bill. I have not read it, but if I were a betting man I would bet ten to one a match was put up against a door, and when the dicks came back in the morning they found the match still there, so there was a charge of adultery and an action for divorce. I will admit that many of these cases are faked, but you do not do that in our courts just by putting a match against a door. You must go a good deal further than that. Ninety per cent of it is fake, and nothing else. I know some suggestion has been made by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) that this thing should be left to the exchequer court; and he got booed in the House of Commons. Of course he does not mind that; he has lived on boos all his life, and by that I mean he has been booing other people, not that people have been booing him.
So we have reached the position where we must admit that ninety per cent of the divorces in Canada are complete fakes. The old saying may be true, that the end justifies the means. My profession was the practice of law, though I had to quit that and go broke when I came down here to attend this House of Commons, with the huge fees we get here. Everybody gets rich once they are elected here; there is no question about that. We do not need a retirement allowance. We get $4,000 a year and we can live for the next forty years on what we save out of that.
The point I am trying to make is that today every man in this house is taking part in a farce. I have no doubt that in Bill No. 106 they had two matches leaning up against the door as proof, which is just sheer nonsense. When a fellow is in that game all he does is leave the place after he has been called on by the dicks, and he leans a match up against

the door. Then the dicks come back the next morning and say, "Nobody came out of that room, because our match is still there."
No one in this House of Commons who has any experience in legal matters will accept this story of the match.
May I state my position? I believe in divorce. I do not mean the Los Angeles or the Reno type or anything of that kind. I am one of those who believe that, as the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) has said, children need a father and a mother. It is only under very difficult circumstances that the parents should be separated. May I do this bit of bragging? I am in the law business and I know there is money in divorce, but I have yet to take one case. I am so annoyed with the whole business. I have made many arrangements by which husband and wife have been able, for a while at least, to get along. I have told people who have no children, "Go ahead and divorce yourselves or shoot one another; do what you like, I don't care. If you have some children, however, they are entitled to a break, and that break is a father and a mother". To me, there is no question of religion attached to it or anything of that kind.
What about the ten commandments?

I suppose the hon. member means that commandment which speaks of coveting. I was not speaking about coveting. It says that thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's wife, nor his ox nor his ass. You thought you had me, but you did not. I am inclined to think that is the commandment the member is thinking about. I shall not enter into that.
I greatly respect the opinion of other people who have equally cogent reasons for a different view from my own. I come back again to this; it should not be a matter dealt with in the other place and confirmed by us so quickly. I have voted for divorce bills in the last six years. I confess I have done that because I think the committee in the other place has done a careful job. Instead of laughing at those men, I believe they have done an excellent and a tiresome job. Irrespective of the amusement we may get in reading the evidence in one of those cases, remember it has ceased to be amusing to those men who are giving their time every morning in the week and many afternoons in the week to listening to this evidence.
Not as much time as you are taking, though.

I am dealing with a hundred, sir, and they deal with them one at a time. That is just an answer to the Minister of Trade and Commerce, because my remarks are confined to Bill No. 106. I do want to say that I think those men are doing a splendid job under difficult circumstances.
Turning to the subject of the bill introduced concerning the exchequer court, I believe that is too much to ask of the exchequer court.
The hon. member might reserve his remarks on that bill for another occasion.
As always, I bow to your ruling. May I close by complimenting those hon. gentlemen who, at their age, may be assumed to have lost interest in that sort of thing, but I doubt it very much.

Mr. Speaker, last Friday during this debate I read the correspondence carried on between Hon. Gray Turgeon and Mr. Manning, the premier of Alberta. For a moment, I should like to review the contents of the reply Mr. Manning made. The first point he brought out was that no bona fide company should be refused incorporation, and that the province should have the right to deal with any of those companies.
