speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture) moved
maintopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to provide changes in the limitation of value determined by the minister in respect to compensation that may be paid owners of slaughtered cattle; to provide additional compensation in respect to certain cattle slaughtered before the commencement of the amending act but after March 31. 1947, and for the repeal of the basis of compensation provisions.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Dion in the chair.

maintopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
The purpose of this bill is to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to provide additional return to those stock owners whose cattle are slaughtered on account of tuberculosis and, when slaughtered, the carcasses are condemned outright as unfit for consumption and on which there is no salvage value. If the amendment were implemented, the return on an animal slaughtered would be approximately the same whether or not it had any salvage value. A higher rate of compensation has been provided for sheep and swine when slaughtered under the provisions of the act. The bill also provides for retroactive payments to stock owners who had carcasses condemned since April 1, 1947. Under all tuberculin test policies it is estimated that approximately 5,329 carcasses will be involved in the retroactive compensation. This number of condemned carcasses resulting from all tuberculin tests since April 1, 1947, originated from approximately 3,553 individual farmers' premises.
I may say that over a long period of years provision has been made for certain payments to be made on livestock that is slaughtered as a result of certain diseases. Certain diseases that affect horses have been covered by this act and certain diseases which affect hogs and sheep, and tuberculosis particularly with regard to cattle. The payments have been approximately the same over the greater part of the period; that is, the possible payments. The act has always stated that a certain limited value could be placed upon purebred stock and lower limited value on grade stock. But the act, as it has been over the years, has stated that the minister or someone on his behalf would set the value that was to be allowed for the stock, but not to exceed two-thirds of this certain valuation; that is, to illustrate, the value of a purebred cattle beast was limited to $150. But the total payment that could be made was only two-thirds
[Mr. Speaker.)
of that. The amendments are asking as the maximum amount the two-thirds of the $150 and two-thirds of the price for grade cattle, and saying that that is the highest amount which can be paid. In other words, the minister or someone acting in his behalf cannot exceed those amounts in setting what the figure is. We do not have to value the animal, then take two-thirds of that, and then take a certain proportion of that two-thirds.
But we do go on to say something which is not provided in the original act. We say that, when an animal is condemned outright and therefore goes into the tank, the payment that is to be made on that animal is the actual valuation based upon the market value of the animal at the time slaughtered.
In order to determine what that value is for the period from April 1, 1947, down to the time this act is declared, we indicate that the method by which the value is determined is the average of the market price over the period of time, rather than trying to determine what the price of an individual animal would have been during that period.
From now on individual animals are dealt with on the basis of the market price. But for the period between April 1, 1947, and the present time that valuation is the average of the prices prevailing on the market over a certain period.
Hon. members may be interested in knowing why we go back to April 1, 1947, or how that date was determined upon. The fact is that during the war we were not carrying on many of these investigations concerning conditions in municipalities, in order to make payments. But since the beginning of April, 1947, we have been expanding our activities in connection with it. We went back to the first month in the year in which, when the act was drafted, a municipality which had been started in that particular month was still being examined into. That month was April of 1947.
When the act was drafted last spring we were still examining into payments which ought to be made in areas where we had started investigations on April 1, 1947. We said there would be discrimination if we dealt with them on any other basis. We go back to April 1, 1947, and make payments right back to that date, which will take in all the counties in Ontario and the municipalities in western Canada where investigations had been started. We are still continuing in those counties or municipalities.
That, I think, pretty well covers the intention of the measure. I have some information with regard to the number of animals affected, and if the committee is interested I shall give that information later.

maintopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
I should like to say a few words in connection with this resolution, which states that it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act to provide changes in the limitation of value determined by the minister. I am not going to elaborate upon the resolution; but, coming from an agricultural riding as I do, and knowing as I do about the tremendous loss to farmers, I am sure this bill will receive a welcome when it is put into effect.
When one part of a riding is within a T.B. test area, and the other part is not, the livestock in the area which does not have the T.B. test have only about half the value. I was informed by some people who had gone to a dairy sale in Winnipeg last fall that the animals they had at home were far superior to those offered at the sale, but that they would not bring the price of those at the sale because they were not in a T.B.-tested area.
When the bill is brought down and compensation is increased from two-thirds of the value to 100 per cent, I know it will go a long way toward helping T.B. areas, and to bring those which are not now in T.B. areas under the act. The reason is that compensation will be given according to the loss on cattle which occurs through condemnation by the doctor.
I am sure that throughout the whole of Canada the bill will receive wholehearted approval. However, there is something else I should like to mention, and that is Bang's disease, which in my opinion should be included in a bill of this kind. Bang's disease has not only destroyed thousands of beef and dairy animals but affected many human beings. Having had a dairy herd of my own some years back I know something of the terrific losses farmers throughout the whole of Canada have sustained from Bang's disease-and not too many people know about it.
This disease in a herd destroys the fertility of the whole herd and, as a result, in a few years one has nothing left with which to carry on. I had a herd of fifty head and, believe it or not, for three years, until the disease was stamped out, I had an increase of only ten or fifteen head. I should like to see the government in the coming year go a long way toward eradicating this terrible disease. It has taken a large toll of cattle and has curtailed the milk flow to all the cities of Canada.
I pass these points on to the government in the hope that they may take action in the future.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I understood the minister to say, during his explanation of the resolution, that the department was not increasing the compensation for animals
Animal Contagious Diseases Act slaughtered. I remember very well statements made by the minister and his parliamentary assistant-

maintopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext: I did not say that we were not increasing payments for animals slaughtered. We did not pay anything before on animals slaughtered and sent to the tank, except an amount which was allowed. But on the animals which do not go into the tank, most of the beef is sold on the market. In addition to what is obtained from the government, the person who delivers the animal gets the value of it as well. Of those that go into the tank, there is nothing-except perhaps the hide and very little more. What we are doing now is to pay the full value of the animal which goes into the tank- which is a great increase over what was paid before.

maintopic: ADDITIONAL COMPENSATION TO OWNERS OF SLAUGHTERED CATTLE
speechtext:
I understand that you are paying full compensation for animals which go into the tank; and on top of that you now say you are going to pay the beef price of that animal going into the tank. Heretofore the salvage value on a tanker has been nil; we realize that.
Previous to the election the minister and his parliamentary assistant made certain promises both inside and outside the house that the compensation paid to T.B. reactors would be increased. A reading of the resolution would seem to indicate that it is intended to change the compensation, but I understand that the valuation is to be lowered to what was paid before, that is, two-thirds of the value.
When this act was first enacted in 1903 the compensation paid was exactly the same as it is today. Under the act as assented to on August 13, 1903, the compensation paid was as follows:
Horses:
Grades, $150.
Purebreds, $300.
Cattle:
Grades, $60.
Purebreds, $150.
Sheep and swine:
Grades, $15.
Purebreds, $50.
Those are the valuations permitted by the present act before this amendment. A new amendment was assented to on June 6, 1913, under which the compensation for grade horses was raised to $200, and for purebreds to $500. The valuation for hogs and sheep remained the same. In 1918 the compensation for grade cattle was raised to $80 and for purebreds, to $250. In 1922 the compensation for purebred cattle was lowered to $200 and the compensation for grade horses was brought down to the old figure of $150, and $300 for purebreds. Then in 1923 the act was amended to its present form.

Animal Contagious Diseases Act
Is it reasonable that the compensation paid in 1949 should be the same as that paid in 1903? Too many times the farmers are expected apparently to bear more than their share of the burden for the benefit of the entire population. I am not suggesting for one moment that the farmers expect to get the total value of animals slaughtered because of T.B. It must be realized that back in 1903 the price of cattle was about one-third what it is today, yet the compensation is the same.
The government says that it is expedient to present a bill to amend the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. The fact is that it has been expedient for the last ten years, but nothing has been done about it. It was very necessary during that time because the price of cattle had increased considerably, and even in 1939 it was going up. The minister suggests that the farmers will be getting enough under this amendment when they receive the beef price for cattle going to the tank. I understand that taking into consideration all districts and all herds the average of cattle sent to the tank is nine per cent and that in very few cases will a farmer lose more than three or four animals to the tank. I have yet to hear of anyone who kicks about the loss of such animals; what the farmers are kicking about is the amount they get for compensation.
It has been only in the last few years, probably in the last three years, that beef prices have gone up to any appreciable extent. Previous to that time I do not suppose that the compensation paid for reactors would any more than cover half the cost of new animals. As I said before, statements have been made both in and outside the house by the minister and his assistant, to the electors of this country and to delegations that have come to Ottawa, that the farmers would get more than they were asking for. I do not think they will feel they are getting more than they are asking for when tley are to receive only the beef price for tankers.
The compensation for sheep and swine is being raised, but that is a different matter as there is generally no salvage value there. No one keeps a diseased animal knowingly because he realizes it is a danger, not only to himself and his family but to any people who might be using raw milk from his herd. These men are interested in the general welfare of the country and are willing to go along with the tests and to see that diseased animals are destroyed. It would be practically impossible to measure the loss to farmers in dollars and cents when animals must be destroyed. A man may have built up a purebred dairy herd over a period of 25 years


and may lose nearly the whole herd. No matter what compensation is paid, such a man suffers a terrific loss.
This is not only a problem for the farmer; it is a national problem. It is a case not only of getting rid of the diseased animal but of getting rid of animals which are disease carriers. The life of every human being in Canada may be affected and it thus becomes a national problem. I think the government should assume a little more of the burden and not place so much of it on the farmer himself. Certainly the compensation paid in the past few years has not come anywhere near covering the losses that have been sustained. I would have hoped that the minister could have seen fit to increase the amount of compensation as was promised prior to the election. As I said before, very few people have ever kicked about cattle that go to the tank. They are complaining about the amount of compensation. The bill is not before us yet, and I do not wish to discuss the matter further until we see the bill and know what its contents are. Therefore I am reserving judgment.

speechtext:
In rising to take part in the debate on the resolution, one of the first things I should like to say is that farmers have been waiting a considerable time for such action. Therefore we welcome the introduction of the resolution regardless of how bitterly we are disappointed in its contents. Apparently there is a vast gap between promise and fulfilment. I can recall that the delegations which came to Ottawa were told that they would receive full compensation, and possibly more than they asked for. If I understand correctly what the farmers of my area are expecting, I must repeat that they are going to be terribly disappointed. My colleague says that the election is over now, but there is another one in the offing. As the hon. member for Brant-Wentworth has said, we want to see the bill before we comment too fully upon it.
Nevertheless I should like to point out three things to the minister and to the house. I think that all Canadians are in accord with

the broad principle of the elimination of bovine tuberculosis from Canadian herds. We welcome that as a health measure. It is a broad public health plan. We hear a lot about what the Department of National Health and Welfare is going to do, and this is only one of the steps that it is necessary to take for the prevention of disease in Canada. I also want to point out that a measure for public health should not be paid for by the farmers alone but by all citizens of Canada.
The minister has attempted to prove to the house that the farmers are not losing a great deal. I have before me a copy of the sales slips of the forty-four head of cattle I mentioned on a previous occasion in the house. They indicate the numbers of the animals, the weight, the price per hundredweight, and the amount the man received. It is only from the dairy herds, the milk cows, that a farmer is going to receive a continuous income through the sale of milk. Therefore I will take the sixteen cows out of the herd of forty-four cattle. Their sale at Canada Packers brought an average value of $91.76. In a previous discussion the minister told us that 10 per cent of the reactors went to the tank. This gentleman was lucky inasmuch as only one of the sixteen went to the tank. If he had been an average farmer, instead of receiving $91.76 he would have received $82.58. If you add to that the $38 that the government pays for these cows, the producer would have had a cash return from each cow of $120.58.
I think everyone knows that it is an impossibility today to buy even a fair grade cow for anywhere near that price. If I were to put the price at $200 I would be putting it conservatively. It would be nearer $240 or more.

Canadian National Railways

speakeroldname: Mr. James Sinclair (Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, those who were members of the last parliament will recognize this as the usual resolution preceding the introduction of a bill providing funds for approved capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railway system. However, I should like to make a short explanation for the benefit of new members, an explanation which needs to be made since the C.N.R. report and budget on which this resolution is based were presented and adopted at the spring session of the last parliament, when the new members of course were not here.
Each year the Minister of Transport presents to parliament the report of the Canadian National Railway system and the auditors' statement on that report. The report for the fiscal year 1948 was presented to parliament by the Minister of Transport on March 18, 1949. The budget for the current year is also presented to parliament by the Minister of Transport, and this year that was done on March 22. Both the report and budget are then referred to the sessional committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government. This year the committee first met on March 21 and had six meetings, calling before it the president and other officers of both the Canadian National Railways and T.C.A., the auditors of the national railway and T.C.A., and other witnesses. The annual report and auditors' report for the year 1948 and the budget for the year 1949 were unanimously approved by this committee in its final report to parliament on April 26, 1949. The present resolution is a natural consequence of the approval of the 1949 C.N.R. budget by this committee. I cannot do better than read the ninth paragraph of the report of the committee which can be obtained, bound with the proceedings of this committee, from the parliamentary library:
The capital budget of the railway system for 1949 includes the following: additions and betterments, $24,500,000; new equipment, $8,700,000; Barraute branch line, $612,890; acquisition of securities and reitrement of capital obligations, $1,692,000; a total of $35,504,890. Against the latter amount there is available from reserves for depreciation and debt discount amortization a sum of $15,738,000, leaving the estimated net capital requirements at $19,766,890.
That is the amount mentioned in this resolution. Since the C.N.R. system is publicly owned, it must now turn to the parliament of Canada for approval to issue securities to obtain this amount of new capital. This is sought in the first part of this resolution, which I shall read. I appreciate that it is a very long resolution, in three main parts. The first part reads:
That it is expedient to bring in a measure to authorize the Canadian National Railway Company

to issue securities not exceeding $19,766,890 in principal amount to provide the moneys necessary to meet capital expenditures made for capital indebtedness incurred during the calendar year 1949; to authorize the governor in council to guarantee the principal and interest of securities issued by the company for the purpose aforesaid;-
The next part of the resolution is as follows:
-to authorize the making of temporary loans to the said company secured by such securities and not exceeding $19,766,890 in principal amount to enable the said company to meet such expenditures and indebtedness;
This part, then, authorizes the government to make temporary loans to the company secured by these securities, to enable the company to meet such expenditures, until the time is deemed suitable to float such an issue. For example, parliament authorized an amount not exceeding $85,882,200 on June 14, 1948, and it was not until September 15, 1949, that an issue of $70 million was floated of 2| per cent coupon bonds, realizing 98-58 to the company. In the interval between June 14, 1948, and September 15, 1949, the government made advances under a similar clause in the 1948 resolution for the approved capital expenditures, which advances were recovered from the proceeds of the loan.
The first two parts of the resolution relate to capital expenditure and capital indebtedness. The third part relates to operating and income charges. This provision may be likened to a revolving fund provided by the government. It is logical to have this provision in connection with a publicly owned corporation such as this, because surpluses in any year have to be turned into the consolidated revenue fund at the end of the year, so the company has no cushion to meet current obligations. Since the budget approved by the parliamentary committee this spring envisages a net deficit of $37,800,000, it is obvious that current revenues of the system will not be sufficient to meet the current operating and income charges throughout the year, so this authority is necessary.	*
The final clause provides that all such current advances shall be reimbursed to the government from the recipients' annual revenues in so far as such revenues are sufficient, any insufficiency to be provided by subsequent deficit appropriation by parliament. I want to make it very clear that this latter deficit appropriation is not covered by this resolution nor is it in the bill which will follow it. When the exact amount of the deficit is known at the end of the C.N.R. fiscal year 1949 a separate resolution and bill will be presented to parliament to make good this deficit; and of course matters relating to the deficit can be discussed at that time.

In summary, therefore, this resolution is presented by the Minister of Finance as a consequence of the unanimous approval given by the sessional committee on railways and shipping owned, operated and controlled by the government, to the 1949 budget of the Canadian National system. It authorized the issuance of securities by the company for the approved capital expenditures in the budget totalling some $19,766,890. It provides that the government may make advances to the company secured by such securities, until such time as those securities are issued. It further provides for temporary loans to the system to meet current operating and income charges, where available revenues are found insufficient, such loans to be recovered out of the annual revenues, or if these are insufficient by deficit appropriation at the next session of parliament.

Various questions have been asked by the hon. member for Wentworth (Mr. Lennard) and the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) relating to Canadian National Railway pensions. An examination of the answers indicates that approximately 60,000 of the Canadian National Railways' employees have no contributory pension and must depend upon the basic pension payable to them at the age of 65, amounting to $25. I feel, however, that this matter of increasing the basic pension does require attention. By comparison with the present cost of living, the $25 basic pension has a purchasing power of approximately one-third of what it had in 1934. When one realizes that there are only 40,700 of the employees who contribute anything to their pension, some 60,000 employees who are working in the lower paid positions in the railway company will receive when they retire only $25 per month with which to support themselves and their wives. Employees who have been superannuated and who are receiving a non-contributory basic pension of $25 per month, number 2,743. Those who are receiving from $25 to $30 per month number 841; those receiving between $30 and $40 per month, number 664. These are extremely minor pensions after twenty-five years of service, particularly when one considers that many of these employees are unable to provide for their own security.
There are some who are contributing a portion of their wages to provide a part of their retirement allowances. Yet, even among those who contribute a portion of their wages and are receiving a retirement allowance based in part on their basic pension and in part on their contributions, there are 476 whose pension ranges from $25 to $30 per month, and 2,095 whose monthly pension is from $30 to $40. The need for action has been brought to the attention of the Minister

Canadian National Railways of Transport by representatives of the railway trainmen who have contended that the rate of pension is too low and is a discouragement to that morale which those who serve on the railway should have.
Many men are being denied a pension to which they would be entitled in part because of the fact that they are unable to establish their proof of age, the census records not being accepted in proof of their age. The regulations should be amended to prevent injustices in this and other cases.
I suggest to the parliamentary assistant that the matter be brought to the attention of the directors of the Canadian National Railways with a view to assuring that an adequate pension or at least an additional pension be provided for the many employees of Canadian National Railways who today are in the position, upon retirement, of receiving only $25 a month.
Mr. William Aspinall of Winnipeg, vicepresident, brotherhood of maintenance of way employees, communicated with the minister last year and, according to a report appearing in the newspaper Labour published in Washington, among other things said that:
The low paid man who has already been retired or will be retired within the next ten or twenty years is the worker who will receive a totally inadequate pension . . .
It was not until 1935 that he was able to make any contribution himself to his pension. Further on he wrote:
The low paid workers, of whom there are many thousands on the C.N.R., are unable to maintain a semblance of a decent standard of living, let alone make a five per cent contribution to a pension plan, particularly the thousands who have families to support.
Mr. Aspinall asked that consideration be given to the increase in the amount of pension. I think this is a matter which deserves the serious attention of the directors of the Canadian National Railways. The total amount of the entire earnings that is today devoted to the payment of pensions is approximately 2-3 per cent, as I have been informed. I realize that there are continuing deficits in the Canadian National Railways. Sometimes it is hard to understand why there should be the large deficit. In 1948, with operating revenues of $491,269,950, the railway had a deficit of $33,532,000, whereas during the years from 1941 to 1945, while operating revenues at no time equalled those of 1948, there was a surplus each year, the highest of which was $35 million. Possibly the solution to meet the problem is that contained in the brief filed by the Canadian National Railways with the royal commission to the effect that the time has come to remove the unfairness that has resulted from saddling the Canadian National
[Mr. Diefenbaker.l

Railways with the overcapitalization resuming in an interest item that may account in considerable measure for the amount of the deficit.
I do not want to ask for expenditures that will increase the deficit, but I feel that this railway company, a national company, owes it to the employees who are unable to make a contribution to a pension for themselves- and I speak particularly on their behalf- that they be not required to retire on a basic pension of $25 a month at age sixty-five. It is unfair. I make this appeal to the parliamentary assistant, without labouring it; I ask that this matter should be reconsidered; and also that the regulations in connection with the administration of the pension should be submitted to the committee on railways and shipping owned by the government so that changes in the regulations may be made so as to remove many of the anomalies which cause discontent and annoyance among railway employees.
While I was looking this matter up I decided to look at the law in effect in the United States. In that country there is a railroad retirement act. The pensions provided for there are considerably larger than those prevailing in Canada. Within the last week or so at the eighth annual meeting of the legislative committee of the brotherhood of firemen and engineers, a recommendation was made that there should be establishment of a national pension plan for railway employees similar to that under the railroad retirement act of the United States. Whether that is so or not, I feel that this is a matter worthy of consideration by the standing committee of parliament. As a national employer, I feel that we should assure to the man that works the same fairness that is being shown by private enterprise, namely, the provision of a fair and reasonable retirement allowance so that when men who have worked over the years find themselves retired at age sixty-five, they should not have to look forward to only $25 a month.
While I am on my feet I should like to mention one other thing in that connection. I have in mind three or four railroad employees who are between forty-five and fifty years of age, who have become ill, are now unemployed and unable to work. I feel that consideration should be given to extending the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act to cover the unemployed period in the payment of benefits to those who by reason of illness or accident are out of work and unable thereby to provide for their families.
I have advanced these suggestions to the parliamentary assistant for the consideration of the board of directors, and also the consideration of the board that administers the

pension fund. I do not think there is any member in the house who would not be willing to serve on a standing committee of the house to consider the matter fully and to revamp the regulations, so that recommendation might be made for an increase in basic pensions to a reasonable figure, and for the removal of anomalies which have the result of causing some employees, who otherwise would be entitled to pension, to be denied it.

Mr. Chairman, I did not rise, as I had intended a moment ago, because I wished the parliamentary assistant to have an opportunity to reply to the hon. member for Lake Centre before I took the liberty of rising to speak about an entirely different question.
In the constituency from which I come we have had a tremendous increase in population over the last thirty years. Today there are four constituencies where there was only one at the time I first had the honour of attending in this chamber. During that period of time, because of the change in the grade of the railway, and the putting in of grade crossings in the eastern end of tne city of Toronto, it has been found necessary to close Riverdale station, one of the two stations which formerly served that area.
At the present time these 300,000 people are serviced by the main union station, which is many miles away from the suburban area.
Canadian National Railways Otherwise they are serviced only with the one station at Danforth, which is neither adequate nor sufficient to look after that population. Furthermore, the population is growing very fast both to the east and to the north of the old Danforth station, so that within a few years we will have there another 100,000 people who will have to be serviced by this old and very small and cramped station. It will be quite unable to give the service necessary for the people living in that area.
It will be only a matter of a few years when it will become a dire necessity to build a station east of Toronto, perhaps in the location of the present Danforth station. The Canadian National Railways now own all that property, which was formerly used as a sorting yard. They have many acres of property there, and at one time a roundhouse was located on it. Most of it is now vacant In due course a new station will have to be built at Danforth to service those people.
I make these remarks to place them on record now, so that consideration may be given as to what eventually should be done. At the same time I would emphasize that in the same very densely populated area there are four level crossings. One by one, as fast as it can be done, these will have to be eliminated of necessity. I speak particularly about the level crossing at Woodbine avenue concerning which an application now rests with the department from Toronto. Then there are the level crossings at Jones avenue and Greenwood avenue, and another one out in the township at Warden avenue.
In approaching this problem I was hopeful it might be treated in a broader sense than simply that of considering the railway and its difficulties and necessities. I thought another requirement in that same community might be hooked up, because for those 200,000 people we have no post office, so called. Of course we have some small postal stations, and some rented premises such as stores and that sort of thing. However there is no post office, as such, or as hon. members would understand post office facilities in a large community.
Further, we have no facilities in that area for the clearing of customs, for excise matters, or matters dealing with the various departments of government which have to be housed. In that western section of Toronto known in the earlier days as Toronto Junction or West Toronto there is a dominion public building which services the community. I know the Minister of Public Works is listening to me because he has heard this story before.
When consideration is given to the building of a new Danforth station, I suggest the

Canadian National Railways Department of Public Works might at the same time consider the proper housing of customs, excise, immigration and post office services, all of which might be housed in conjunction witih the new station, and in one substantial public building to serve this fastgrowing community.
I address my remarks to the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance, whom I commend for his concise statement of a few moments ago, and also put on record some suggestions to be considered bv the Department of Public Works. After all, the money comes from the treasury, and it would be unfortunate if these two problems were to be considered separately. The Canadian National Railways own the land, and that land would offer a logical location for the other services i have mentioned. I was anxious to place this position on the record and in due course, perhaps during the spring session, we may be told whether anything is going to be done. When the Minister of Public Works is dealing with his estimates perhaps he will indicate that he will give some consideration to the inadequacy of the services presently available in the eastern section of Toronto.

Indeed the hon. member was perfectly justified in basing his remarks upon the need for good morale and the highest efficiency in the national system.
It is hardly necessary fcr me to say how thoroughly I support the piea for the best possible deal for our railroad workers in the matter of pensions and pension rights; after all, I have raised such matter., times without number. Nevertheless the parliamentary assistant greeted this as though it were almost a new subject, which makes it evident that we must bring this problem to the attention of the government in every possible way.


I feel that strong support should be given, certainly on an interim basis, to the plea that the basic pension of $25 per month be increased, and indeed that there be improvements right across the board in the Canadian National pension regulations. I must say that they are a little better than some of the other railway pensions in effect in this country, but that does not mean that they are satisfactory. I hope it will not take too many pleas of this kind; T hope it will not be necessary to raise this matter year in and yea- >.ut Defore there is any improvement in me pension position of Canadian National employees.
I was glad the hon. member for Lake Centre had got hold of the United States railroad retirement act, and has looked into it and found what a good piece of legislation it is. I am glad that the hon. member now joins with me in suggesting that something of this nature should be brought into being in this country. It seems to me that here we get a little beyond a matter which the parliamentary assistant will say should be brought to the attention of the management of the railroad; here we get to something that is a matter of government policy. One of the things that appeal to me about this proposal of a railroad retirement act in this country is that it is something that the federal government could initiate without having to go through this dominion-provincial squabble. So far as labour relations are concerned, railroad workers come under federal jurisdiction. We hear talk all over the country and all over this house about everyone wanting to move in the direction of over-all social security, and I shall speak about that again on another occasion, but when it gets down to the question of doing something, the old problem of the constitution is always trotted out. That is not necessary so far as workers who come under federal labour jurisdiction are concerned.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take advantage of this first opportunity I have had to congratulate the parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance upon his presentation of this resolution. One part has to do with the estimated capital expenditures of the Canadian National Railways and the other part has to do with unspecified advances to the Canadian National Railways and affiliated railway and steamship companies for operating deficits, and similar advances to Trans-Canada Air Lines to cover operating deficits in this year.
I have before me the reports of the committee on railways and shipping which sat this year to review the annual reports of the Canadian National and the Trans-Canada Air Lines, together with the budgets of the two
Canadian National Railways systems. There are certain features in the resolution now before the committee which do not necessarily follow from the annual report adopted by that committee and recommended to the house last year. I should like to ask the parliamentary assistant some questions arising out of those discrepancies. In the first place, what capital expenditures are to be incurred calling for the advancing by the government to the C.N.R. of nearly $20 million? If they are not capital expenditures, then what capital indebtedness is expected to be incurred? If it is capital indebtedness for replacement of equipment, will the parliamentary assistant give us some indication as to what extent it is not covered by depreciation in the ordinary way? That covers the first part of the resolution.
Coming to the second part dealing with the anticipated operating deficit of the Canadian National Railways, the budget of the railways indicated an estimated net deficit for the current calendar year of $37,800,000. I beg your pardon-

After all they have the credit of the government of Canada and of the Canadian nation behind them. Therefore

Canadian National Railways they could borrow in the normal way of business if they had a slight excess in their deficit over what was anticipated and what was authorized by the advance to them from parliament. I should like the parliamentary assistant to answer the question why we are not given a specific sum in the second part of the resolution so far as the C.N.R. and subsidiary or connecting companies are concerned. subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
I shall only be a few minutes. As one who was employed in industry for twenty-six years, I have done a lot of thinking, talking and reading on the subject during that time. Pension schemes are inadequate throughout industry as a whole. In most industries there are no pension schemes. If we intend to find a solution to the problem it is not going to be done in the way suggested by the hon. member for Lake Centre or the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. These palliatives must be retained until something better replaces them. We will be talking in the same way about industrial pensions one hundred years from now if we follow the course of action we have been. For example, in industry across Canada you have differentials in wages. You


have large companies which make profits and can afford to pay adequate pensions. You have smaller companies which cannot afford to pay a decent pension. They can show you that by their balance sheets. Then there are essential industries that are uneconomic and have to be subsidized by the government. They cannot pay anything.
If you take all the basic industries of Canada, that is the position you find yourself in. If you maintain the practice of trying to provide for workers in industry on the basis of the workers and the corporations getting together to solve the problem, there is no solution for it. The Canadian National Railways must come before parliament every year for the purpose of having the taxpayers of Canada wipe out a deficit. I think it is rather nonsensical to ask them to increase their pensions, wage rates, and so forth. That is the problem that has to be solved. Every worker has one fear, the fear of insecurity. Where do I go from here after I reach the end of my years of productivity? If you can solve that problem you will have solved one of the major problems affecting all workers of Canada, farmers, fishermen and industrial workers. It is not going to be solved by trying to place the responsibility on industry and the workers themselves.
There are good examples right now in the United States. The coal industry has been practically paralysed for several months. They are wrangling in the steel industry. They are coming out of it in some kind of way at the present time, but they will repeat the performance next year. There is only one answer to the problem. If you intend to provide some kind of pension, and nothing under $100 a month is worth while, there is only one way it can be done fairly so as to equalize both the payment and the contribution, and that is by taxation. If the government of this country think that when workers reach a certain age, and have been in a given industry for a certain period of time, they should have a retiring allowance, then they should work out a social security tax for that purpose.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext: On a contributory basis.

subtopic: PROVISION TO MEET CERTAIN EXPENDITURES AND GUARANTEE OF SECURITIES AND INDEBTEDNESS
speechtext:
You will be contributing when you pay your taxes. Everyone would pay an equal amount into that fund, and everyone would share equally in it when they reached the retiring age. Then you would have one national administration handling the fund. As it is now, with these piecemeal arrangements as between industry and industry, you have overlapping and millions of dollars wasted in administration, which a government department would offset. Unless we

get down to thinking in those terms, in my opinion we are wasting time; there is no solution. On the basis of their balance sheets the Canadian National Railways are not in a position to pay any more, as far as I can see; and in the final analysis it is the taxpayers who have to bear the cost of wiping out this deficit year after year. I believe we have to get down to business and think more or less along these lines. It is simple enough; tax everyone, so that everyone contributes and everyone shares. You will have one administration, which will simplify bookkeeping and be more efficient.
I have lost interest in these business and industrial pensions. I know where the mine worker winds up. I know where the steel worker winds up-on the scrap heap, with a broken back. That is the thing that worries him all his life. He carries about $500 insurance, enough to bury him. He tries to pay for that, but there is no hope for anything at the end of the trail except a worn-out, broken body. Thousands of workers are in that position today. I merely make these observations in order that hon. members may come to think of these matters along these lines. The pulp and paper industry of this country has established a decent pension of $100 a month. That industry can afford to do so. If a man passes away and his wife is left behind she receives a death benefit of $2,500, and all the contributions her husband made are paid back plus interest.

The hon. member's second question was why there was no limit in the second part of the resolution, that part which I described as providing a revolving fund. The C.N.R. deficit, of course, is only estimated at the amount mentioned, $37,800,000. It is quite true that this amount could be specifically mentioned in the resolution and in the bill, but I repeat that it is only an estimate. The hon. member mentioned that if by any chance

Canadian National Railways this estimate was exceeded, the C.N.R. could follow the ordinary practice of borrowing. However, the C.N.R. cannot borrow from banks in the way other railways can; it is limited to borrowing from the government, as a check on its borrowings. I want to say that the steel company in Hamilton, Imperial Oil and various pulp and paper companies have made great contributions, unasked, without the use of force and without strikes, in an endeavour to provide security for the people who work for them.
I appreciate, and I agree with the hon. member, that this is not good enough. We must make it more general. I was going to refer to those who sit around me. I used to be able to mention those who sit opposite me, but now I am reminded of the charge of the light brigade, who had cannon to the right of them, cannon to the left of them and cannon behind them which volleyed and thundered. These fellows who shoot from my back I know do not intend to shoot me in the back, but they cannot speak from any other position than that which they have been assigned because of this tremendous majority of Grits in this House of Commons. So I say once more that I think this is the
IMr. Sinclair.]

point the hon. member had in mind: we must devise some contributory scheme, be it by taxation or otherwise, by means of which we shall solve this whole problem of old age. Perhaps it is not altogether a problem of old age, but through injury or something of that sort there are those who have not the energy or the ability to keep themselves and their families. I had in mind some monthly or quarterly contributions.
I turn now to this resolution directly, and I think of something I said this afternoon, but I shall not quote that, Mr. Chairman, because I know there is a rule forbidding one from quoting anything said in a previous debate. I think the principle is the same, however. What we are doing is not so much considering these few dollars, although they are in the millions. I have been here long enough to know that a million does not amount to much, I mean broadly speaking; I do not understand it myself. At some time, we must come to the point of fixing this stupid capital structure of the Canadian National Railways.
This afternoon we did the same thing as we did in the past when we took over a bunch of broken railways. The man who put that through was Arthur Meighen who, in my judgment, is one of the greatest statesmen that ever lived. Putting that measure through killed him politically, but he was the man who did it. We found a lot of individual railways who could not look after themselves and we had Mr. Hanna, since gone, take them over. I was his personal solicitor, and if any of you knew him you can imagine some of the difficulties I had.
Later, in the history of this railway, we got Sir Henry Thornton. He bought a hotel in Paris for a million dollars. We needed that hotel as much as I need a third leg. Perhaps I need a third leg more because I have one bad knee, but we needed the hotel about as much as you normal fellows need a third leg. He did a great service, though. For the first time, he made a railway. Sir Henry Thornton put spirit into that company. He was expensive, but he put spirit into the Canadian National Railways, for which I think he will be long revered and long remembered. I am going to say this to the parliamentary assistant to the minister and to the Minister of Transport who, happily, is in his seat. I do not want any wrong inference drawn from that statement-I think he is more in his seat than any other minister, so I am complimenting him on that. What we have to do is solve this problem. Do we want to sit here year after year-

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext:
I hope it may be possible to have this resolution passed tonight so that the bill may be distributed and discussion may take place on the second reading and in committee.
The Emergency Gold Mining Assistance Act was passed to provide assistance to the mines in defraying part of the post-war increase in the cost of production during the years 1948, 1949, and 1950, during the time that the product they were producing was selling at a fixed price. It has been of great assistance to the mines and has enabled some of them to continue in operation where they would otherwise have been forced to cease production, with resulting hardships to mining areas.
Experience has shown that some amendments to that act are desirable, and the amendments that are proposed come under three headings. The original act provided assistance on gold produced in excess of two-thirds of the production in the base year; that is, in the year ended June 30, 1947. The first amendment provides that assistance will be payable to mines when, through no fault of their own, production has decreased below production of the base year. Assistance will be payable on one-third of total production in such cases. I may say that several mines have continued in operation in expectation that this legislation will be passed.
The second amendment in this bill is necessary because of the difficulty that occurs when gold is produced in concentrates. In some cases mines produce gold in concentrates during one year, but do not reduce the concentrates into bullion until a later year. As a result, costs of production of an ounce of gold have been considerably lowered in the year the bullion is produced, while the heavy costs of production take place in years when the ore is taken from the mine. This amendment provides that the governor in council may regulate the manner in which
the costs of production shall be calculated, so that the assistance payment will be truly related to the actual cost of producing the gold.

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext: Do you mean that, on gold produced several years ago and kept, you are going to go back?

subtopic: AMENDMENT OF ACT RESPECTING EMERGENCY
speechtext:
No; gold which has been mined in one year and is in concentrate form and has not been reduced from the concentrate to bullion until a later year. It is much cheaper to produce gold bullion from the concentrate than it is to mine the ore. Consequently, the gold bullion will be related back to the year in which the ore was produced.
The third amendment recognizes the adjustment in the exchange value of the Canadian dollar and provides for the reduction in the amount of assistance payable to any mine during the year 1950, by an amount equal to $3.50 for each ounce of gold to which the rate of assistance applies. This amending act is to be retroactive to June 15, 1948, when the original bill came into force.
